utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could we please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everybody in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours to my learned colleagues from the Defence and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis for the Prosecution assisted by my case manager, Alma Imamovic-Ivanov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much and for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, good afternoon to my colleagues from the OTP. To everyone in and around the courtroom. I'm Vasvija Vidovic with Nicholas Robson representing General Rasim Delic with legal assistant Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon to you sir. And I'm sorry to have kept you waiting and standing. May you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dedovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I move to my questions, I would like to ask you to speak as slowly as possible and to leave a pause between my question and your answer because in that way, we will have a complete transcript and it will reflect everything that we are saying here.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are aware that what you are saying is being interpreted and also my question and your answer should not overlap.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you for your full name for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I am Ismet Dedovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo on the 28th of June, 1965.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where do you live?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I live in Sarajevo, in Dervis Numic Street, number 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And which school did you complete?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I completed the technical engineering school.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, where were you when the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you join any army?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning of the war, I joined the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it will be better if you move closer to the microphone. At any point, did you become a member of the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was on the 12th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And which duties were you performing?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I was an escort of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who decided to appoint you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The decision on my appointment was made by the military security administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So did I understand you correctly, that you were part of General Rasim Delic's cabinet?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where was General Delic's office when you began to work there in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic's office was in the building off the directorate of the construction company.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name of the company.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name of the company, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the Vranica Construction Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also speak up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where was the Vranica head office?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The Vranica head office was in Sarajevo, in the Centar municipality, centre municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember where the offices of the operation centre of the Main Staff were at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The premises of the Main Staff operations office was in the public accounting services building, and it's known as the building near Vjecna Vatra, the eternal fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify because it's not quite clearly entered in the transcript. Can you please repeat? I asked you about the operations centre of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the operation centre of the Main Staff was in the building of the public accounting office which was known as the building near the Vjecna Vatra.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. How far was the office from this place where the operation centre was. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was some 4 to 500 metres from the commander's office.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to ask you to something about the scope of your work. You told us that you were appointed as escort of the Main Staff commander. How long did you work as General Delic's escort. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, of course. How can I not? I worked at that post throughout the whole war and then after the war until the General retired except for a certain period when I went for military training.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, you were an escort of General Delic from the point in time that he became the Main Staff commander until the end of the war. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain to us how much time when you were doing this job did you actually spend with him?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the work is of such a nature that I was practically with him for 24 hours a day. I was with him all the time expect for the time when the General was sleeping, but even then I was immediately close to him. I was in the next room.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us exactly what your duties were, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: My duty was to provide security for the commander when he was in certain places or when he was moving.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain what you mean when you say "to provide security for the commander in a certain location.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: This means that one would know which unit was securing the facility where the commander was staying, how many soldiers there are, what the shifts are. My own duty was to be in front of the office and to -- well, all the visits to the commander were announced, so I knew about each single visit.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what does it mean to secure the commander while he was moving?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: This meant that we would announce that the commander was about to go somewhere for a visit to a unit or to a different location, so this would be movement with vehicles, helicopters, or walking. I was his private -- on his private security detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any duties in relation to the commander's visits to specific locations?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would announce that the commander would be coming to specific places or facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whom did you inform about that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the corps commander, if he was visiting the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will come back to this. I just want to ask you this: Did you have information about the communications facilities used by the commander if he used any?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, our communications devices were quite poor. They were just normal radio sets, radio stations which we couldn't even use properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Because the devices of the former JNA were exceptionally powerful so they would cover us electronically. They would override us so we were not able to establish communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the B and H army at that time, did they have just devices?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. The quality of our devices was quite poor. The army of the Republika Srpska actually took over all the equipment of the former army, so they had the latest technology and we only actually had some left overs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Are we talking about -- you mentioned announcing visits when you would be going out in the field. Did the commander tour units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Delic spent a lot of time touring the armija units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how many units there were in the B and H army at the brigade level, and I'm talking about the period from mid-1993 until the end of the war. Do you have an idea on average how many such units there were?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: There were about 100 brigades, on average, and also there were about 500 battalion-rank units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please tell us who choose the units, if anyone did, that the General would visit. How was this process conducted?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the process was that the corps commander would decide which unit would be presented to General Delic, and if it wasn't the corps commander it was his deputy or his chief. Commander Delic did not decide which unit he would visit. It was a decision made by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move to a different topic now. I would like to talk to you about some events from June and July 1993. You told us that you were appointed as escort of General Delic on the 12th of June, 1993. I would like you to describe for us the situation in the General Staff or the Main Staff, the way you saw it when you came to take up your duties as escort of General Delic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The situation at the Supreme Command staff was very unfavorable for General Delic. There was a lot of distrust directed at him. His closest associates felt like that. At that time he was their superior officer so at any point they were trying to obstruct the General's work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the witness to look at Exhibit 216 now, please. This is a document under seal, so can we please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, a moment ago you mentioned the Sarajevo commanders who, you said, did not support General Delic. Can you tell us briefly, please, what you had in mind when you said that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: They formally recognised him as commander but did not carry out his orders. I was referring to the members of the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was their relationship vis-a-vis the commander of the 1st Corps, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle, they did not respect the commander of the 1st Corps or the commander of the staff. They did not feel obliged toward them in any way, and did not have any respect for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned these commanders who were local commanders from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to see the situation, what it was like when it came to the other BH army units in that period of time just before you took up your duties in the office and afterwards?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had occasion to see that. The units of were highly disorganised. The commanders were local commanders. Every street had its own commander. The command and control system had not been established among these units, and this made it possible for the commanders to act willfully and not have to respond to the -- their superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were there instances of crime in and around Sarajevo? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The highest presence of crime in Sarajevo was that of the black market, smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the issue of crime, to your knowledge were certain activities taken after the -- General Delic took up his duties? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon taking up his duties, the General took certain measures which meant that at once strong cooperation was developed with Mr. Bakir Alispahic, the minister of the interior. They met on a daily basis and worked a great deal toward combatting the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt a little bit. When you say the crime was rife in Sarajevo with respect to smuggling, are you talking of amongst the general public or within the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It had to do both with the civilian and military structures. Everyone was smuggling throughout the town. Everyone was involved in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Including members of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Some members of the army, not the army as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat one name for us now. In your earlier answer you explained that the General establishes cooperation with the minister. Can you please slowly and clearly repeat his name? Can you spell it out, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The minister concerned was the minister of the interior, Bakir, B-a-k-i-r, Alispahic, A-l-i-s-p-a-h-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown video 26, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, you heard the comment made in this video-clip. If the minister of the interior or the Commander Rasim Delic issue an order, everyone has to abide by it. We have an example out from the field where Commander Delic signed a piece of paper of his. He say, well this is all in vain until my superior officer signs. This nobody will consider it seriously do you have a comment to make on this?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What we just saw precisely reflects the situation as it was in the field. There were brigade commanders acting willfully, not respecting the commander of the 1st Corps, the minister of the interior, the commander of the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the minister of the interior, Bakir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I omitted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this. The speaker said Fikret is the boss on that side of the Igman mount and on this side, Hadzija is the boss. First of all can you tell what you say this means, the other side or the slope of Igman mountain, and Hadzija, who are these people?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is Tadic, the commander of the 4th Motorised Brigade, Fikret Prevljak; and Hadzija is Ismet Hadzic, who was the commander of the 5th Motorised Brigade; and they were the ones who practically had a say as to who could come into the town or leave it. They were the ones exercising control over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you remind you to stop after a while after hearing the question to allow the interpreters. You overlap and the interpreter is moving very fast to catch up with you. I think she missed a few things.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can this video-clip be assigned an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Video 26 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the video becomes exhibit 1356.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, you described some aspects of the situation in Sarajevo, and the problems encountered in the command system. Can you now explain to us very briefly what the military situation around Sarajevo was in June of 1993 if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And that was the most difficult part of 1993, because in early June the Serb forces launched powerful offensive in the direction of the town of Gorazde. They surrounded Gorazde which caused the exodus of the Drina valley population, people fleeing in large numbers. There were many refugees. However, the Serb forces did not stop there. They advanced toward yet smaller town of Trnovo, but they did not stop there either. They approached the Jahorina villages and the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Another location the witness mentioned, the interpreter didn't catch.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: There was fierce fighting around the town. Everyday artillery fire incriminate fire on the towns, fire opened upon all the intersections. The living conditions in the town were very poor. There was no running water, electricity, food, or medicines. Everything was in short supply.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, just for the transcript we want to clarify something. You mentioned a plateau. Can you please tell us the name of the plateau?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The Bjelasnica-Treskavica plateau. That includes the mountains of Treskavica and Bjelasnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please spell the name the plateau?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The Bjelasnica-Treskavica plateau, B-J-E-L-A-S-N-I-C-A T-R-E-S-K-A-V-I-C-A.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where this plateau is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It is very close to Sarajevo. It's known as the Olympic mountains.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this situation and these events relating to Igman, did you notice or not any activities in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a lot of activity for the commander, especially there were meetings with the 1st Corps commander to resolve the situations that were arising. There was a large number of meetings with representatives of the international forces with the UN commander of Bosnia and Herzegovina forces. I think that the General's name was Briquemont. And there were daily activities plus the internal problems within the staff itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you this now. You said that you were always in General Delic's escort. At that time did you try to leave in July 1993. Did you try to get out of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we tried to get out of Sarajevo but that was practically impossible then because it was the strongest enemy offensive at that time on Sarajevo and the wider Sarajevo area. We tried to get out. We stayed outside for a couple of hours, and then we returned to Sarajevo. The commander wanted to see for himself what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you not manage to get out then?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Because of strong enemy fire, because the way out of Sarajevo through Igman was constantly under the control of -- or tank fire from the direction of Gavrica Brdo, antiaircraft guns from the direction of the forestry school, they held that sector of the Igman road and they opened fire, so it was impossible to get out of Sarajevo. The only way to get out would be at night when the lights were turned off using the Macadam forest road. But it was still practically impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to ask you this now. When did you actually manage or did you at any point succeed to reach free territory and when, if you can recall this?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first time we left was towards the end of August 1993. And that is when we went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe how this crossing of the Igman mountain was like?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was just like I described it earlier. It was very amazing thing to get out of Sarajevo without lights. It was like playing Russian roulette. If you passed, you passed, and if you couldn't pass, it meant you were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you got out sometime in late August 1993. Can you please tell me what was your experience of the situation in the field in Zenica, for example, in August 1993, how did you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The situation was the same or similar to the one in Sarajevo. The communications were not functioning well with the Supreme Command staff. The units were not linked up. Personnel was inadequate at command posts meaning that people who were leading those units were not properly trained in order to be up to the task.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you find all of this out?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: During lunch, during a visit to the command of the 3rd Corps, General Enver Hadzihasanovic, I know that General Hadzihasanovic complained to Commander Delic that they didn't have enough materiel, equipment, ammunition, food, and General Delic replied that the situation was the same there all units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you actually know that there was HVO in the Central Bosnia sector at that time. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the situation vis-a-vis the HVO? What were relations like the HVO like at that time. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time the conflict escalated between members of the HVO and members of the B and H army around Zepce, Vakuf, Vitez, Kiseljak, and Mostar, these were all the actual areas that they held.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And were new a position to talk to General Delic about the events at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: During the driving, the commander would talk about it, so I actually learned what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to go back to this. I would just like to ask you to repeat again the names of the towns where the clashes broke out with the HVO at that time. Can you please speak slowly and clearly.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: There were clashes in -- there was an exchange of fire and the situation escalated in the areas held by members of the HVO, and this was in Zepce, Gornji Vakuf, --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please say Zepce again?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Z-E-P-C-E, Zepce; Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Vitez, Kiseljak, Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we have all of this on the transcript now. I interpreted you with my request to repeat the names, so you said in response to my question, if you had talked about some events with General Delic and you said that you did have an opportunity to hear about the events while talking with him.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, these were more comments by the commander than a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would just like now to go back to some events in Sarajevo very briefly. You talked about insubordinate commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to show the witness for a moment Exhibit 217, please. Your Honours, before the document is shown on the monitor, I just wanted to say that the Bosnian version is not very legible the way it's been scanned, so we have prepared the document. Before we show it to the witness, I would just like to show it to my colleagues from the Prosecution. For the transcript, this is a criminal report of the Security Administration from the 29th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please look at page 5 of the Bosnian version. And this is page 3 of the English version. Page 3 of the English version. Mr. Dedovic, You mentioned insubordinate commanders and we have a description here. Can you please look at this part on page 5 which says on the 2nd and 3rd of July, 1993, as members of the 10th Mountain Brigade of the 1st Corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the 9th Motorised Brigade participated in the armed attacks on the buildings and members of the public security service Stari Grad centre Sarajevo? You were a member of the Supreme Command so does this text reflect the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the document does reflect the situation as it was in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on that day you worked at the Supreme Command Staff this was the night between the 2nd and 3rd of July. Was anything attacked in the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the operation centre of the Supreme Command Staff was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you this now. Did you know the son of General Delic, Admir Delic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 7 of the document now which is five of the English version, page 5 of the English version?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: While we turn the page, could we have elicited from the witness who attacked the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Supreme Command staff or, rather, the operation centre was attacked by members of the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So can you please look at halfway of the paragraph where it says: "Members of the 10th Brigade arrested the following military police officers, Delic Admir, Ibrahim Greda, so on and so forth. Do you know who this person is Admir Delic who is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Admir Delic is the son of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, did something like that happen to the General's son?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes what is said here did actually happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe what you know about that event?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. This is largely irrelevant to the charges facing the accused, and I don't see exactly why we need to be going into what happened to the accused's son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I absolutely disagree. This particular detail is very relevant, and it is very illustrative of the situation in which -- actually it is very relevant for the indictment. This is June 1993, July 1993, so it's relative in terms of the indictment when General Delic is receiving letters. This is the situation in which General Delic was acting, and this is the situation that indicates his influence as a commander. This is going to be quite clear in the next two or three questions. The Supreme Command staff is being attacked, and his son is arrested. So if this is not relevant for the situation in which he was acting and for the situation -- or actually for the Court's understanding of how powerless he was to do anything in that situation, then ... Your Honours, actually, I cannot understand the nature of the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question will be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before that, I just have a correction for the transcript. I was speaking quickly so they did not manage to put it in. I put in the time in which the -- General Delic allegedly received documents and not received documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we were interrupted. I would just like to ask you if you recall my question.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you answer?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, go ahead?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Admir Delic and Greda Ibrahim were arrested by members of the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigade while they were carrying out their regular assignments. They were brought to their headquarters. Their IDs were confiscated and then they could see exactly who these persons were as soon as they found out that it was General Delic's son, they began to abuse him, insult him, beat him. They took their uniforms from them and gave them worn torn clothes to wear, and after that, they were taken to dig trenches. During the interrogation, Greda Ibrahim and Admir Delic at some point managed to escape to the part of the building that was under the control of the Egyptian Battalion. They were then arrested by members of the Egyptian Battalion and returned to members of the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigade and then they beat them up even more.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: To your knowledge, was General Delic able to have any sort of influence on this situation involving his son?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic could not have any influence on this situation for any course of action. He had to ask for the approval of the superior structure, and that was the Presidency and the president of the republic. The commander could not take any action on his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want the witness to be shown D937.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you see on the screen is a document dated the 5th of July, 1993, and it's a medical certificate belonging to Admir Delic. Please have a look at it. Is this document related to the events you described?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document is related to the event which took place. However, I see that his injuries were very much downplayed in this medical certificate, because the injuries Admir Delic sustained were far more severe than described here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what is your interpretation of this answer?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how I see it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection. This is both irrelevant, and I fail to see how the accused's body-guard can interpreter a medical certificate. So we object both on the grounds that this is completely irrelevant to these charges, and certainly the accused's body-guard is not in a position to comment or interpret a medical certificate in our respective submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know how it was interpreted. I did not ask the witness to interpret this medical certificate, although this is how you may see it on the transcript. I wanted the witness to interpret or tell us to interpret his own words to us, to tell us what it is that he meant when he said that the medical certificate was downplayed. I was interested in his answer and not in the medical certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When she is now going to tell us about the downplaying of the certificate he is beginning to comment on this document, and I really don't know whether he is a person to comment on this document. I think the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ultimately, yes, Your Honour. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my objection still stands to this entire line of questioning. It is one thing to say that incidents concerning the 9th and 10th the Defence position being that they were not under control. It is a completely entirely different matter to be going into these injuries sustained by the accused's son that has nothing to do in our respectful view with the issues concerning this trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was meaning to respond to this, and I apologise. I didn't see that you were conferring there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Would you like to respond now? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant to say that I had already explained the position of the Defence because the Prosecutor repeated the objection that was raised earlier on. And I had, at that point, responded why I believed the line of questioning was highly relevant and I was referring to all the questions, save for the last one that I withdrew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic. We understand that you may have had a point in making -- telling us what happened on the 9th and 10th -- is it the 9th and 10th? But I really think, and I think this is the view of the Bench that you're going a little too far. We've heard that the accused's son was arrested, was beaten up. What are we going to could with this medical certificate, for instance, what are we going to do with the extend of his injuries? If you tell us he was beaten up and the accused therefore had to go and attend to him, that's enough, but to tell us the extent of the injuries, I don't think it is absolutely relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I want the document to be assigned an exhibit number and the point, why I want this document to be admitted, is neither what the Prosecutor claims here nor what you inferred. Now, the point of the matter is not whether the accused was supposed to go and see his son but the extent to which the accused had influence to wield and what the situation was like within the command and control system as he took up his duties and what his position in that was. In the context of his son being arrested, and for this reason, Your Honour, I would like this document to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, if you wanted to have this document admitted, just say so. When you give all that argument, I'm not sure whether you are commenting on the ruling that has been made or not and that would not be appropriate or permissible, to comment on a ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would again object on the grounds that this is not relevant. The medical certificate is not relevant to these proceedings, and we say that all due respect both to the accused and to his son. The fact of the matter is issues concerning command and control even as they related to the 9th and 10th Mountain Brigades in Sarajevo. That issue is separate from this medical issue, this medical certificate and what happened to the accused's son. And this document and this line of questioning is not relevant in our respectful submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is not going to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, did you hear of an individual called Senad Pecar?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether something was happening that involved this person?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time Senad Pecar was taken into the military security office and he was one of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat his duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter asked that the witness repeat the duty of this person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Senad Pecar was assistant commander of the 10th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this might be the good time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We still have some three minutes, Madam Vidovic. Unless you're saying you're going into a new topic and you don't want to break it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I resume my examination of the witness, I would like to state the following for the record. During the testimony of the earlier witness, General Karavelic, we received an order to change an exhibit MFI 1334, or, rather, we were ordered to change the translation by adding one word. This was a piece of video footage, if you recall, MFI 1334. We corrected the error in the translation and sent the video-clip to the Prosecution and the chamber, as well as the registrar. And can the number of the Exhibit MFI 1334 now be changed? Can it be given another exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we were provided a DVD with this video. We'll take a look at it perhaps at the next break if not any sooner. I don't think we can access it here in the courtroom, and I think it is fine at that point based on Madam Vidovic's assurances and if there is an problem I will come back to you, but I think it might cleaner at this point to go ahead and admit the document, strike the MFI and if there is a problem then I will revisit the issue, if that is acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. MFI 1334 is now admitted into evidence and it is Exhibit 1334. Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, we spoke of Senad Pecar. You said that you knew who he was. Can you tell us briefly what was going on after his arrest. Do you have any knowledge about this and why did you mention him having been arrested.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Senad Pecar was arrested and taken to the military security office. At that point in time, we were right outside the Security Administration building when the chief of the military administration, Fikret Muslimovic the president's escort Haris Lukovac and two more officers of the military security sector were commenting upon the arrest of Senad Pecar. There were two members from the 10th Mountain Brigade there as well. Through a hand held radio set, Musan Topalovic, Caco, spoke -- Musan Topalovic spoke to someone from the Presidency and it boiled down to this. He was threatening that unless Senad Pecar was released right away, he would be using mortars to shell the Presidency building. He also threatened to abandoned the defence line held by his brigade. We then went to the Presidency building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who had arrested -- what's his name -- Senad Pecar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Senad Pecar was arrested by members of the military security service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of their actions that I already mentioned. Some criminal activities from earlier on, attacks on public security stations and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He was part of Caco's clique?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was one of the deputies of Musan Topalovic, Caco.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said we were outside the Presidency building and then you said we went into the Presidency building. Who is we?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The Commander Rasim Delic, and I as his escort.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us what happened next, if anything happened?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic attended a meeting with the president. I don't know what the meeting was about. I did not attend such meetings. I do know that as we returned to the command Senad Pecar was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did General Delic have any information about this case?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't have any information about the case. We were taken aback by it. The commander was quite poorly informed of all the goings-on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You say we were taken aback. Why was this the case?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Because the commander didn't have any information about these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who did?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Presidency had the relevant information. They turned to the president for all the problems they had. They did not recognise the commander of the 1st Corps as their immediate superior or the commander of the staff of the Supreme Command. They did not recognise them. For any problems they had, they turned to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move on to a different topic now. In your evidence you said that the command post of the staff of the Supreme Command was in a building in the centre of Sarajevo. Did there come a time when a command post of the staff of the Supreme Command was set up outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In early 1994, in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, how often did General Delic go to Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Very rarely. Only if we were on a route to other corps that we would visit. He only went to Kakanj rarely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown video 28 now, please. Video 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what was mentioned here was that part of the staff was operative in Kakanj and part was operative in Sarajevo and that they communicated only through occasional visits and correspond but that there were not many opportunities to meet up. This is what the speaker said. What is your comment in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: This shows that the commander spent very little of his time in Kakanj to meet up with his subordinates. They didn't have occasion to meet often.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How long would the General stay in Kakanj, if he stayed there at all?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes 15 minutes, sometimes two hours or one hour, sometimes -- actually, not ever a whole day but more or less a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this video-clip be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, who was the first speaker?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness the Judge is asking you --

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff, General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Enver Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The video clip V 28 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours video 28 will become Exhibit number 1357.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've already told us that you were near General Delic. Can you please tell me, after the Kakanj command post was established, what were the activities of General Delic? Can you please describe that the way you saw it, as his escort?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: After Kakanj was established, General Delic had a lot of work. There were a lot of duties, and most often this consisted of negotiations with members of the HVO, the establishment of a lasting truce and the cessation of hostilities. There were also lots of meetings with representatives of international community and members of the HVO and all of this brought about the Zagreb agreement and this was, I think, on the 28th of February, 1994. He was fully engaged in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So let's clarify for the transcript. It's not all there. Here you're talking about the period after the establishment of the Kakanj forward command post?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is January and February 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like you to just tell us briefly as follows. You said that General Delic worked on this agreement with the Croats. After the agreement, were there any activities that you know of?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After that, General Delic was even busier on joint cooperation of the army of the B and H and the HVO and the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the witness now look at D986, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't overlap, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. For the transcript, this is a part of the daily information bulletin on the 11th of January, 1995. Can we please scroll down that -- so that we see the bottom of the document in the Bosnian version and also can we zoom in on the part of the text in the Bosnian version -- the part of the text in the lower right-hand corner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, now can you please look at this. The title is Delic-Rose talks. Can you please tell us who was this person Rose, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This was British General Michael Rose commander of the UNPROFOR forces for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did General Rose meet with this person from what you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, General Rose and General Delic met frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the second page of this document, also in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in the section in the middle where it says: "The military attache, US military attache visits General Delic? Witness, can you please look at that section of the text. The next talks about a meeting that had to do with the implementation of the military part of the Washington Agreement. I would like to ask you if you know whether this visit by the US military attache was an exception in this period or did something like this happen frequently, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. The US military attache's visit was not an exception. He would come by quite often. Not just him, all the accredited military attaches in Bosnia would often come and visit the commander as well as representatives of international organisations the Red Cross. They would all come to talk with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit number 1358.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the witness now look at D991, please. For the transcript, what will be interesting to us is this bottom right-hand corner. General Delic -- actually, the whole section, both of the text in the lower right-hand corner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to ask you this: This is the press centre release of the 15th of March, 1995 of the army where it says General Delic received Ambassador Preinsing and then also the military attache of the Republic of France?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how much time General Delic actually spent with these people?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Quite a lot of time. They would come to visit the commander often. They would be interested in the implementation of the peace accords, cooperation with the Croatian Defence Council, the Croatian Army how this was being implemented and the implementation of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this exhibit please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, before we decide on the admission of this document, I have a question that relates to this and in fact also the former document, namely to understand the relevance to it. Does the witness know whether any matters relevant to the indictment were discussed during these meetings or what is otherwise the purpose of bringing them to us, other than showing that General Delic was a busy man, which I fully believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'm going to be very brief without influencing the witness in any way. This speaks to, in part, about what you said, about what the General was doing but what's important also are the dates of these documents. They could be very relevant in indicating where General Delic was, for example. That he wasn't in Kakanj but that he was here. So the dates of these documents and the dates of these visits are very important to us, as well as the fact that we can see what we can -- what General Delic was doing as a commander at the strategic level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is exactly what -- what bothers me a bit. Because I don't see what he was doing as a staff commander. I see that he was doing something, that he was talking to Johannes Preinsing or other military diplomates or military ones. But what they were talking about is not obvious from these two bulletins.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, based on these two bulletins, the way I see it we can see that this is military diplomacy this is involved. But we will have a couple of witness who perhaps would be able to throw more light on these documents and meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit number 1359.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, I would now like to focus on some events from June and July 1995. Before I move to June and July 1995, I would like to ask you if you recall the situation in the town of Sarajevo in the spring and summer of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The situation in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo was critical. We were exposed to constant artillery fire. There was a large number of civilian victims. There were shortages of food electricity, water, and this led to further developments whereby all of these things had to be resolved. So that was when plans were made to lift the blockade of the town of Sarajevo. So this went on until sometime in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that there were plans to lift the blockade of Sarajevo. Do you know anything about who ordered the planning of these activities to lift the blockade?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The Presidency as the supreme commander of the army headed by the president, adopted this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember hearing any views expressed by General Delic relating to this decision?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that the commander made a comment that this was not the time to carry out such a broad operation because the armija at that point in time did not have enough materiel and equipment for such an extensive action. There were shortages of everything, artillery, ammunition, infantry ammunition, medical personnel that would be needed at times like that. So we were not quite ready but the commander had to carry out the superior's orders, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you recall what the role of General Delic was in that action?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic's role was to plan and lead or control the action.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, if you remember, how long the operation lasted?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The Sarajevo operation went on from early June until the end of August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how involved General Delic was in this action?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: He was very engaged and involved in all areas relating to this action.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did this mean practically? Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Practically this meant that he was constantly at forward command posts, that he was touring the corps -- the corps units in order to establish the best possible coordination among units during combat actions to control the activities and this called for permanent activities by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And were you with him all the time throughout that whole action?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was with him the whole time of the action.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you left Sarajevo in order to have the General command the combat actions? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Early June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And after that, did you return to Sarajevo? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, for some three or four months, we returned to Sarajevo once. The rest of the time we spent with the units. The commander was directly involved in combat actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe what this was like, what was he doing? Was he stationed in one place, did he move from place to place? Can you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was like this. You cannot be in one place and still manage or lead the whole operation. We kept changing locations constantly, moving from the forward command post at Prokociva Visoko then the Nisici plateau, and in order to tour all of those places without stopping for long, just from Visocica from Proskok you would need some seven to eight hours travelling on the road the way they were then. Then it was also a very complex operation, which meant that we were constantly on the move.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please, do you remember whether General Delic received or did not receive any documents during the action?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, General Delic did not receive any documents in that period because that is something that would have been handed to me first, so, for sure, he didn't receive any documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So General Delic was evidently absent. So how did the staff function, according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Just like any other staff, the commander, of course, has his deputies, he has the Chief of Staff. They all are carrying out their own assignments, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, I fail to understand what the witness has just told us, because in my -- in my understanding, it would be very difficult to -- to lead a major operation of this kind without receiving or indeed sending any documents from the units that worked under his command. So I would like you to explain to the Court how -- how the communication was done then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through the direct participation of the commander in the action he was able to do that. There was no need for the reports to be sent to him because he was out in the field. We toured all the locations where combat activities were ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I'm sure that -- that all the units in the corps and the brigade and the battalions would send documents up through the system, documents that were intended to reach General Delic. So how did he get that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The General did not receive that information. If the information did arrive, it reached the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And would the Chief of Staff then relay orally the information to General Delic? Is that how it functioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that, because I was not present when these conversations would take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us for the sake of the record slowly, please, what were these locations where you said the corps had its forward command posts, or you also mentioned the locations General Delic visited. Can you take them one by one slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Proskok, a location on Mount Igman; Visocica, just above Visoko; Orahovo, above Ilijas; and the Nisici plateau.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. To your knowledge, when did the combat activities relating to the lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo gain momentum? When did they come to a head?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was between the 10th and the 17th of July, 1995. That was the time when the fighting was at its highest.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall where it was in that period of time you mentioned, between the 10th and the 17th of July of 1995, that General Delic was to be found?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, we were visiting parts of the Sarajevo battlefield. All that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Proskok and Visocica how far were these locations from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: To reach Visocica from Proskok, and the circumstances and conditions at the time and the roads in place it took you some seven to eight hours to make the journey.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I misunderstood your answer. But let me ask you this: What is the distance between Visocica and Proskok on the one hand and Sarajevo on the other?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know as the crow flies or along the roadways.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I mean along the roadways that enabled you to reach Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I meant when I said some seven to eight hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will be referring to July 1995. Did you learn of some events taking place in Eastern Bosnia at that time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we heard of the exodus of the Eastern Bosnia region that massacre had been committed on the civilian population and that an exodus of the civilian population took place not only in Srebrenica and Zepa both of which were UN protected areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how General Delic came to learn about these events?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic learnt about these events through the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did he take any action or do anything in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Since at that point in time the commander was preoccupied with the Sarajevo action, some five to seven days later, we set out for the Tuzla region. That's to say into the AOR of the 2nd Corps where the commander stayed in Kladanj and Tuzla where refugees were coming in as well as the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was some seven days later so the 18th or the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Of which year?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did General Delic do in fact in the areas of Kladanj and Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We were in the area where civilians were coming in and the commander spoke to them. These were situations of grave hardship when you see the wounded, individuals whose entire families were killed, when you spoke to people who managed to survive these atrocities. It was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what it was that happened later on, after the 19th and the 20th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We went to Split and stayed there some two to three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say, "we went to Split," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic and I.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the witness now be shown D1005, 1005. For the record, this is an excerpt from the daily information bulletin of the BH army for the date of the 23rd of July, 1995. And can you please zoom in on the bottom right column in the Bosnian version. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You see that the text reads: Yesterday, in Split a meeting of the delegations from Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatian joint declaration prepared. You told us that you went to Split together with General Delic and do you recall what the -- the motive of that visit was?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was precisely the Split declaration as it came to be known later which meant the strengthening of the relations between the Croatian army and the BH army and achievement of peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how long the negotiations took?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Two to three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this document be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit number 1360.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, do you remember where you went next after Split?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We went to Krajina to the Bihac region, to the Una-Sana area, which was under strong enemy activity at the time; and the fighters there had to fight two fronts, one was against the fors of Fikret Abdic and the other was against the Serb forces and they were in a very dire situation. They were almost faced with the same fate as befell those in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the forces of Fikret Abdic and this wasn't entered in the transcript, did you mention that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Fikret Abdic's forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours anything about these forces, what do you mean when you say they were faced with two different enemies?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the one hand you had Fikret Abdic, who enjoyed the support of forces from Serbia. He had members of the White Tigers and Arkan's men on his side. They enjoyed support from Serbia, and the other enemy was member of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Not earn in the courtroom is familiar with Fikret Abdic. Can you tell us who he is?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: He was a the self-proclaimed of -- president of the self-proclaimed autonomous province of western Bosnia. They set up their own army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what General Delic was doing at this time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: He was quite busy with the activities in Krajina precisely. This meant that he to set up defence line there and everything else that it entailed, and in doing so he had the support of the Croatian forces. What did this mean? In that period of time we went often to Zagreb to visit General Zvonimir Cervenko, I recall this quite well. And this had to do the cooperation between the two armies in that geographic area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to repeat the General of the Croatian army's name?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: General Zvonimir Cervenko.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recall whether there were any visits abroad in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were part of an extended military delegation that visited Iran for some five to six days. Upon our return from Iran, Commander Rasim Delic had meetings with representatives of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us look at document D1020, and then I will have some other questions for you. For the record, this is another excerpt from the daily information bulletin issued from the press centre of the army dated 2nd of September, 1995. Can we zoom in on the first bit of the document in the Bosnian version, the delegation of the BH army in Iran. The 28th of August is mentioned here. Were you referring to a visit to Iran in this time-period or --

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was precisely the time-period when this visit took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be assigned an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, as you may sense, the Chamber is, again, hesitating, because we are not sure we understand the relevance of this document. If you, as I suspect you might, seek introduction of this document into evidence because of the fact that General Delic was away between 28 August to 31st of August and thus was not present in Sarajevo, then my question to you would be: Is this -- should I then infer that General Delic was not in command during those days, or what is the impact that you want to -- to lead out of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was the time when preparations were taking place for the action that is the subject of the indictment. The Prosecutor alleged that General Delic had preliminary information early on about the preparations that were taking place for this action. What I'm trying to show with this is where General Delic was in fact at that point in time and what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But the fact that he was physically abroad, does that, in the view of the Defence, imply that he was not in control of what happened during those days when he was absent?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, yes. The Defence, at that time, he was represented by other persons and also this document is important to us. The dates are important, just for the sake of information or knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You did not ask for the admission?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did, Your Honour. I am waiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I challenge you to show me where you asked on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on my screen it's on page 47, line 19, I think. Yes, 19 and 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit number 1361.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I apologise, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like the witness to look at Exhibit D1021, please. For the transcript, it's an article from the Vecernje Novine daily for the 2nd and 3rd of September, 1995. And the article is entitled Delic- Cervenko meeting, successful and useful cooperation. Witness do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before, you mentioned that General Delic after returning from Iran met with General Cervenko. Can you please comment whether this was at this time?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was precisely at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the dates here, the 2nd and the 3rd of September?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The 2nd and the 3rd of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours can the document be given a exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit number 1362.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, have I been putting many questions to you that I am aware that you might have difficulty recollecting the answers to, but I would like to ask you the following. You recall that until the 3rd of September, according to this article and then after returning from Iran you stayed in Zagreb for two or three days?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened after that? Do you remember what General Delic was doing, what happened after the 3rd of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We came back to tour the Sarajevo front. We spent a couple of days there and then after that, I think, on the 8th or 9th of September, we went to Malaysia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us again where you went?
