utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We went to Malaysia, because at the time, there was a conference of Islamic countries for assistance to Bosnia and Herzegovina that was being held in Malaysia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how long this flight lasted? First of all, I want to ask you this, do you remember when the conference began?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the conference began on the 9th of September, and it went on until the 16th of September. The trip to the destination, the actual flight, took some 13 or 13 and a half hours. We had to leave one day early in order to get to the conference in time. Actually, we got there a day before it began.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say you arrived the day before the conference, that means --

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: That means the 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what General Delic was doing during the conference?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The General was very busy. He was fully involved because all the Islamic countries representatives who were taking part in the conference wanted to speak with the commander about the kind of help needed by Bosnia and Herzegovina which would not have survived at that time without the assistance of Islamic countries. So they all wished individually or as a delegation to speak with the General, which the commander, of course, made possible for them. He devoted his whole time to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this now: In your testimony so far, you said that you were travelling with the General outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I want to ask you this: Were there any contacts between General Delic and yourself with his office while he was absent? Was there any contact with his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. There was no contact by General Delic either with his office or his subordinates, because if he had wanted to get in touch with anyone, he would have done it through me. I would have made that connection. But talking with the office or the corps command in those conditions, I mean, it was an open line, it could have been tapped, so the General is a cautious man; so he was very careful about things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: Why would he inform you? Why would he have asked you to set the connection up?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, General Delic did not speak English, so it was up to me then for that reason to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your knowledge, during the stay in Malaysia did the General have any contacts with his subordinates?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't. He had wanted to get in touch with them, he would have done it with my assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who did you have to speak English to, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Asking for the dialing codes and to have an outside line from the country where you were in required some talking. We didn't have any kind of portable or satellite telephones in order to establish communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dialing codes you get on hotel literature. He could just read that himself. He doesn't need to talk to anyone to get that, does he? He knows the dialing code for Sarajevo, and he would know it even from Malaysia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no, the commander, as a rule, did not actually do the dialing himself or establishing of the communications. This was something that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That is a different story. Sorry, the problem was not English, the problem was there was protocol.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was just actually about to ask that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Other than English, was there any other reason why you would do that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the security point of view, and the topic of the conversation, that was something that he had to take into consideration in view that it was an open line, whether he wanted to risk that or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any rules of your own? Just wait a little bit, please. Take it slowly. Just wait for me to finish. You, as General Delic's escort, did you have your own rules that you had to respect?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you something else now. During this trip to Malaysia, do you remember if the General had maps, if he took any maps with him?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, General Delic did not carry any maps with him. I was carrying his personal items. It was just a brief case where General Delic kept a notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't carry any maps in that brief case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no maps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the witness look at Exhibit 1078 now, please. For the transcript, this is an excerpt from the duty operations officer for the 14th and 15th of September, 1995. From the duty operation officer's diary for those dates.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this paragraph, Mr. Dedovic. Can you read what it says in paragraph marked with the number 4?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I quote it for you what it says is that at 1900 hours BH army commander General Delic rang and asked about the situation in the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps this was at 1900 hours on the 14th/15th September 1995. You said that General Delic did not initiate any contacts. Can you comment on what it says here, in this document?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can comment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether he said he can or cannot comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps I can assist. My question was not precisely noted down in the transcript, if this is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I just want to clarify my question to you. Testifying you said that General Delic did not establish contacts by telephone with his subordinates. There was a call recorded here and an alleged call by General Delic. I would like you to comment on that, if you can.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the first part of the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of that, the state of health of General Delic at the time who had an elevated blood sugar our team that went to Malaysia also included a doctor Bosanko Horozic, who was a diabetes specialist so what I want to say with this. I want to say that General Delic had to take medicines on time in view of the time distance which was some six to seven hours, meaning that our time, if it was 1900 hours in Malaysia it was then 2.00 in the morning. That means that according to all of this and in view of the activities that the commander had over those days, at that time he definitely would not have been able to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, there are a number of confusing issues for me around this discussion and this document. First of all, I don't think what the witness said now answers the question you asked. And I don't see how relevant it is to the question. Secondly, we have just been told that this is a duty officer's diary. I don't know duty -- and I see there is 3rd Corps at the bottom. I don't know where this duty officer is stationed and on what day is this telephone discussion. I know you have said it is 14th/15th of September and -- okay. So General Delic would have been in Malaysia at the time. Can we just get the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I will, Your Honours. Obviously the transcript did not catch the first part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please, I asked you if you can comment on this part of this document that refers to the telephone call or, rather, a call, telephone call by General Delic which was received by the 3rd Corps at 1900 hours. And you answered but the first part of your answer was not included in the transcript, and the interpreters noted that in the transcript. Please, can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time and it had to do with the conference in view of the fact that General Delic was suffering from diabetes we had a doctor with us in our team his name was Bosanko Horozic, who was a specialist for diabetes. The commander was being administered insulin, so in view of the activities that he was performing over those few days he was quite busy and if we take into account the time difference, 1900 hours here, is 2.00 in the mourning in Malaysia, so in that time-period, the commander was probably sleeping. He didn't have any activities because he had to stick to doctor's instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours if I can say I don't know what is happening the witness is answering quite clearly, but the answer is not being correctly reflected I don't know if it is the interpretation or what it is. It does not reflect what the witness is saying. It's very confusing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, the whole story about General Delic's condition and health while in Kuala Lumpur has nothing to do with the question you put. It may very well be that the witness has given an answer. If can you ask him to give a short concise and relevant answer to your question, please. He is asked to comment on the fact that he testified that General Delic didn't normally make calls now there is a record of a call. What has his health got to do with the question? I would think you should control your witness too, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness is answering what the connection is, but the transcript does not reflect that. That is the problem. The witness is saying that the man was sick and that he was asleep at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you please simply say what you were explaining now. Why are you mention a doctor. Why are you mentioning this?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Because the General was sticking to the instructions of the doctor in view of the seven hour time difference in view of the fact that it was 2.00 a.m. in Malaysia and 7.00 p.m. in Bosnia at the time, this cannot stand, because the General's definitely asleep at that time, and I want to add something else. In principle if the commander even spoke, he would talk with the corps commanders not with duty operations officers. He asked for information firsthand. He would not ask information from the duty centre. I mean, it's a question of how much information they would have available.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, let me just hold this piece of answer. I don't know, one, where the witness gets 2.00 a.m. and 7.00 p.m. because there call was made at 9.30 in the morning, number one or what is it. Sorry, 7.00 in the evening, okay, fair enough. Is the answer is that -- is the witness denying that this call could have been made by General Delic is that the purpose of all this explanation, because he was asleep at that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you answer this, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the time difference. When it was 7 p.m. local time, it was 2.00 a.m. in Malaysia, and I know that the commander was sleeping at such wee hours. He was not making phone calls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You see that had never come up. It is coming up now for the first time, after three or four attempts. I mean, I'm talking about the English part of it. Yes, you may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: In connection with Malaysia and the trip General Delic made, how did the journalists and the public at large in Bosnia and Herzegovina view this. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They had a negative view of all the visits undertaken by General Delic at the time. They would make statements to the effect that General Delic was travelling around the world while Bosnia was at war, which shows that they simply did not grasp what it was that he was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this might be the right time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, before the break, we left off as I was asking you about the reaction on the part of the media and the public at large to the trips that General Delic undertook in September 1995. And I would like now to show the witness D768. It's a document from the moral guidance administration dated 24th of September, 1995. I apologise, it's Exhibit 768; my apologies. The document is titled information on the negative publicity in some of the media. Can the witness be shown page 3 of the document, please. The second paragraph in the Bosnian version, which is page 2, the last paragraph on that page of the English version. Page 2 of the English version and page 3 of the Bosnian version. Thank you. Witness, I'll direct your attention to the second paragraph, which reads: "The authority of the commander of the General Staff, army General Rasim Delic, was treated with open irony in an article entitled "Sala Masala" what a joke by Sead Fetahagic in Oslobodjenje of 18 September 1995 and similarly in an article entitled 51 per cent of Bosnia and Herzegovina liberated by Senad Avdic in Slobodna Bosna, issue 2, 21 September 1995. The following inappropriate comparison was made: Dudakovic almost in Banja Luka, Delic almost in Kuala Lumpur. Do you recall this, witness?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this text reflect the reaction on the part of the media?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether General Delic made any statements for the media thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was it about?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was in relation to such texts and head lines that General Delic was trying to justify his actions before the mass media. But this was all due to the fact that they did not in fact know what General Delic's mission had been, as I already stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on what you can remember, when was it that returned from Malaysia?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We came back from Malaysia on the 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall where it was that you went next?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We went to the area of Bosnian Krajina where there was fierce fighting going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When I asked you about where it was that you arrived, I meant by plane.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We landed in Zagreb where the commander met with representatives of the Croatian army again, and after that meeting, we returned to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown Exhibit 1292. Exhibit 1292.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, look at the preamble of the document. You see that the date is the 20th of September. Look at the initial part of the document, or, rather, can I read it out for you. A summit meeting was held in Zagreb on the 19 September 1995 between delegations from the republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and army General Rasim Delic and Croatia Mr. Franjo Tudjman, Mr. Susak and General Cervenko in the presence of Mr. Holbrooke, General Clark, Mr. Galbraith, US ambassador to Croatian and the mediator for the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Robert Owen. You a moment ago that you landed in Zagreb where General Delic had some meetings?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was precisely to these meetings that I was referring.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the names -- the meeting mentioned in this document? Witness, please speak up, I know you're tired by now.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how long you stayed in Zagreb in relation to these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe we stayed there for two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document can now be put away, please. Do you remember going somewhere after the 19th of September, 1995? You said a moment ago that you returned to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Specifically to the Bihac area where there were combat activities carried out by our units in that time-period.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say that combat activities were being conducted. Did everything go to plan?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not everything went to plan because the coordination between the BH army forces and the Croatian army forces was not that good, and General Delic's task was to ensure that the level of coordination between the respective armies was as good as could be achieved.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown Exhibit 1038. Your Honours, I apologise. It is not an exhibit; it's a D document. D1038. As you can see, it's a photograph. Mr. Dedovic, do you see the photograph clearly.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you assist us by telling us whether you can recognise anyone on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Do I need to indicate the individuals?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. I'll ask you to identify the persons here one by one. I want the electronic pen to be handed to you.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: General Atif Dudakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you place number 1 above his head.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Head of office, Ferid Buljubasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The second escort?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Ajhan, army General Rasim Delic. And this is me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Person number 5 is you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that the photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was in early Autumn 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you told us that you went to the Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was the photograph made at the time or in a different time-period?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was made precisely in that time-period.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact location but it was in the general area of Bihac. I wouldn't be able to tell you the specific location.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember how long you stayed in the area with General Delic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We stayed there for a couple of days. Next, we visited Zenica and Zavidovici which was on or around the 22nd or 23rd of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you stayed in Zenica and Zavidovici for?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was a very short stay because we visited the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you visited the 2nd Corps, where was that exactly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We went into the AOR of the 2nd Corps, specifically to the -- to a part of the Vozuca battlefield Petrovo Selo, which was in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall the events following your visit to Zenica? Did you go to Sarajevo, or elsewhere, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I think the commander returned to Sarajevo where he had meetings with representatives of the international community. This was the period immediately preceding the signing of the Dayton Accord, and he a great many meetings with representatives of international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I proceed, I would like the photograph to receive an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis. Mr. President we have no objection to the photograph going in, but I would ask perhaps it is not clear from the transcript the witness marked the numbers one through five, indicated a number of names, but I think he only tied two of those names to the actual numbers on the photographs but perhaps if he could again just clearly indicate who is -- who's who of the names for each of the numbers that would perhaps be helpful. Madam Vidovic, do you think you can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, and I thank my colleague Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you answer these questions, please who does number one refer to on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Number 1 is division army General Atif Dudakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Atif Dudakovic is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who does normal two relate to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Head of office of the commander, Colonel Ferid Buljubasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who -- number 3 refers to on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The second escort --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the name of the second escort because it is not reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Akova Ajhan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that the name of the second escort.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Akova Ajhan. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And number 4, who does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Army General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And number 5, who does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Ismet Dedovic, who was the personal escort of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that's me. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Then the photograph will be admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the photograph will be admitted as Exhibit 1363.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And before you proceed, Madam Vidovic, I just want to ask a clarification question to the witness. Sir, before Mr. Mundis stood up, you said that you think that the commander returned to Sarajevo where he had meetings with representatives of the international community because that was just before the signing of the Dayton Accord. My question to you is where did you and -- and the second escort go to when he went to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was with General Delic throughout that whole trip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. It's just that -- thank you very much. It's just that you said that he went and all this time you have been saying we went. You may proceed, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is something that I, too, wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, I would like to ask you something about Vozuca. Earlier you mentioned that General Delic was in the Vozuca area. I think you mentioned on the 22nd of September. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this: You told us that you were constantly with General Delic. In July, August, September, or October, did you notice General Delic's activities that pertained to the Vozuca pocket action, other than that one visit?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. From what I know, General Delic had no activities relating to Vozuca. We didn't even stay in that area except on the 22nd of September. That was the area of responsibility of the 2nd Corps, not the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the witness to look at video 32 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps while that's coming up it is unclear whether the last photograph was actually tendered and/or admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was admitted as exhibit 1363, Mr. Mundis. Thank you. What are we now playing? Video 32.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, I would like to ask you this: Do you recognise this situation that we have just seen in this video footage?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in the escort of General Delic during this event?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you this now. For a long time -- you spent a long time with General Delic, most of the war. Please, how did you experience what his attitude was towards the civilian population and towards prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: At any point when addressing soldiers, General Delic emphasised the fact that you had to act in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, strictly according to the Geneva Convention rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to ask whether that question is necessary now that he has seen the video anyway. We've got that evidence already from the video. But you may proceed. You have asked a question. Yes, answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to have this video admitted as part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, who is the General speaking to, when was it, and where was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dedovic, can you please answer this question?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic gave a speech to the newly formed mixed artillery unit in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the year?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And when exactly in 1995 was it? Which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was September 1995, I think. Late September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mid-September 1995. And where was the speech given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact location, but I know it was in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just intervene. The witness said late September. I don't know, perhaps you received the interpretation as mid-September 1995 and you know General Delic was not there. The witness said late September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it was just Judge Harhoff not Judge Moloto who was speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But this was then shortly after the Vozuca operation, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the very end of the month of September 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But tell us, Mr. Dedovic, why would the General remind the newly formed regiment about the duties to respect the Geneva Conventions if that was after a major battle. I mean, this sounds to be me to be a speech that the commander would hold just before a major operation were to be launched, he's telling his soldiers that now we're going to this operation and please do not forget to respect the Geneva Conventions. That would be the gist of the speech. So that is why I'm curious to know where are we -- and why was he holding this speech? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander, on any occasion not just on the occasion of this speech but on any occasion he would emphasise that the behaviour has to be strictly in accordance to Geneva Convention rules in respect of civilians and prisoners of war. He would emphasise that on any occasion, not just on this speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe, Madam Vidovic, you can help me out, because I need to understand why we are seeing this. I accept that the General would remind his people to of course respect the laws of the war, but it is in -- in proximity to these operations that took place in September 1995 and it is within the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps. So has this anything to do with the crimes charged in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this speech does not have anything to do with parts of the indictment, and I believe that this witness said -- I don't believe that this witness said that he knows anything about Vozuca. I think it was just the opposite. The -- he did not deal with Vozuca at all except for the visit that he talked about. The General is charged under the indictment and one of his duties and general duties was to instruct his subordinates about conduct in war conditions, in accordance with provisions of international humanitarian law and that is why I am presenting this evidence here now. I am putting that to the witness, who knows this for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I accept that, Madam Vidovic. It's just that you can't -- you can't help the Judges or at least you can't help one Judge thinking that it is strange that, on the one hand, we are told that the General did not have any role in the performance of the Vozuca operation, and yet you choose to present us with a video that shows that he was in the area of responsibility, speaking to a newly formed regiment in the 3rd Corps, at the same time or approximately at the same time when these actions took place. So you are kindly requested to explain to us then what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honour, this event that is being shown in the video the witness indicates that took place in late September. The Vozuca action took place considerably earlier, according to the indictment, Your Honour. What the General is being charged with took place earlier. Therefore, I really don't see any connection in this context that you are speaking about the witness said that this event took place in the Zenica area. The witness is not connecting this video with the Vozuca events at all. Possibly you didn't understand that. And the actions of the 3rd Corps can in no way be connected only with the Vozuca area. We're talking about a vast area in this case. Your Honours, I apologise, I apologise, my colleague is suggesting that a part of the witness's answer is not reflected in the transcript, but I cannot help in this. The witness definitely did mention that Zenica that the video is from the Zenica area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need some clarification regarding this video-clip. It may be that I didn't understand properly. But, Witness, you told us, and please correct me if I'm wrong, you told us that after the meeting in Zagreb on the 22nd of September, you went together with General Delic to Sarajevo where he was very busy with negotiations and so forth. Did you understand that properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But now we see him in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps and that's end of September. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't remember the date when this footage was made, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the exact date, but I know that it was the end of September, definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that he didn't stay all that time in Sarajevo, that he moved about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is only one exit from Sarajevo in the course of those activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I just want to say a little concern I have at the back of my mind which arises from your explanation why you want this video in, I understand that General Delic had the responsibility to do what he has just done, but I also know that he is not charged with failing to do that job. He is charged with crimes that are committed by his subordinates. So that's why I tend to share the concern that Judge Harhoff was raising with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I tender this video into evidence but it is of course down to you to make the ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The video is admitted in into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video will become exhibit number 1364.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dedovic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My name is Daryl Mundis. I represent the Prosecution in this case. I have a number of questions for you. I want to stress at the outset, sir, that if you don't understand any of my questions just ask me to repeat them, and I will rephrase the question. Can you tell us, sir, a little bit about any military training that you obtained or received prior to the outbreak of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the former Yugoslav people's army, I was a member of a special purpose unit. I have been training in various sports, and I had been training Judo for more than 20 years. Before the war broke out, I had military experience from the JNA that was at the level of an ordinary private.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you tell us, sir, that you been in this special purpose unit in the JNA, can you tell us a little bit about what that special purpose unit was and what type of training you had received?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: This was a reconnaissance/sabotage unit to be precise, that special purpose unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what kind of training did you receive to become a member of this reconnaissance/sabotage unit?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the criterion of the then-National Defence secretariats was on the basis of which they assigned conscripts to various specialties. I had been a sportsman myself before joining the service, so maybe that was part of the decision there, because part of the training concerned was also that in martial arts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time, sir, that you were appointed as a body-guard or escort to General Delic, did you hold any rank?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: There were no ranks in the army at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time, sir, that ranks were initiated in the ARBiH, what rank, if any, were you given?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Initially, my rank was second lieutenant, and I ended my career with the rank of a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, during the course of the war while you were serving as body-guard or escort to General Delic, did you or were you sent for any additional military training?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, not during the war. After the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it, sir, that because of this position you held, you were never -- during the course of the war, you were personally never a commander of any type, in terms of commanding any type of unit?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any combat unit under my command, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you told us in -- identifying a number of people on Exhibit 1363, the photograph, you told us about a second escort, Akova Ajhan, I believe his name was. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He was hired periodically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. That anticipates my next question but let me ask it anyway. Were the two of you the sole body-guards for General Delic during the war, or were there other people as well who performed this task?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: His son was among the escort of General Delic. Admir Delic was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, so, just so that we're clear when you say the escort of General Delic, are you telling us that Admir Delic, General Delic's son, also served as a body-guard or when you use the term escort are you referring to something else?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: He was also in -- he was also part of the service providing security for General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than providing security for General Delic, what other functions did Admir Delic carry out during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: That was his only duty or function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us that this person Akova Ajhan was hired periodically. Can you tell how frequently he was hired? Was it some of the time, most of the time, very rarely, almost always?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So on all other occasions other than these very rare occasions when Mr. Ajhan was involved, you and Admir Delic constituted the sole security team, close protection team for General Delic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that you were with General Delic virtually all of the time. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Throughout the war, I was with General Delic throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now let me just run through a series of different scenarios if you will and tell us if you would typically have been with General Delic during such situations. When General Delic was having meetings, would you generally be present in those meetings or would you wait outside of the room where the meeting was?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, I didn't attend meetings, conversations or anything of the sort. This was not part of my job. I waited for the General outside the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, you were aware, were you not, that General Delic, during the war was a member of the extended Presidency?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. General Delic was a member of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you then, to your knowledge, General Delic, when he was in Sarajevo, attended the meetings of the War Presidency, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When it was possible for him to attend, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when General Delic attended the meetings of the War Presidency, were you in the room or did you wait outside of the room?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody was admitted into the room, save for the Presidency members. I was always outside of that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, when -- let's talk about other types of meetings. When General Delic would have meetings with, for example, his Chief of Staff, General Enver Hadzihasanovic, would you be present for those types of meetings just General Delic and General Hadzihasanovic, the two of them meeting, would you be present, or would you be outside of the room?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never personally attended the General's meetings with anyone. My duty was always to be outside of the room where the meeting was taking place, not in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you ever personally present, Mr. Dedovic, when there were of any discussions or plans for military operations that General Delic attended?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never attended the planning of any actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, sir, about a number of occasions when General Delic was outside of Sarajevo, and you specifically indicated or talked about a number of meetings with corps commanders. Is that -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir -- do you recall, sir, being present when General Delic met with any of these corps commanders? For example, General Mahmuljin were you ever present when the two of them had a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never present in the room where they discussed any activities. I was never in such a room together with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How about during this visit to the Bihac area where there was a photograph of General Delic with Commander Dudakovic. Do you ever recall attending or being present when General Delic met with General Dudakovic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never attended their meetings or their conversations. This was always behind closed doors. It was not my job to be present -- during such conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about any meetings between General Delic and the 1st Corps commander, General Karavelic, were you ever, sir, personally present when General Delic was meeting with General Karavelic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Generally speaking of all of these meetings that you have been referring to, I was never present at any of them, and I was always outside of the rooms where they were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about meeting, sir, with journalists? Are you aware of the fact that General Delic may have met with journalists during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He did meet with them, because following such meetings they would normally hold press conferences to let the public know what the meetings were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you ever personally present, sir, when General Delic gave interviews to journalists, just a one-on-one kind of interview, perhaps in General Delic's office?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not in the commander's office while he was making press statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand what you're saying, sir, is when people would come to see General Delic in his office, you would not be present in those meetings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never attended these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that would be regardless of the fact of whether the visitor was a member of the military or a civilian or a journalist or any other type of person?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was never there. My only duty was to announce their visit to General Delic. Other than that, I was never present at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when General Delic was travelling outside of Sarajevo, sir, do you recall any occasion at any location where you personally were in the room when General Delic was having a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never was present in the same room where General Delic had a meeting with someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And we've talked about the corps commanders or at least a few of them. Does the same hold true, sir, with respect to any other military leaders that General Delic might have met with? That is, you were not present when General Delic met with any other military leaders or commanders?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I had never attended any sort of discussions with officers at any level of the command cadres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about any meetings that General Delic had with political or civilian authorities? Were you ever present outside of Sarajevo at any such meetings?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not present in the meeting rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about meetings, sir, when you travelled with General Delic abroad? Let's focus on that. Do you recall, sir, at any point in time when you were travelling abroad whether you were personally present when General Delic had meetings with any foreign military leaders outside the Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, General Delic did have meetings with both military representatives, representatives of NATO, but I did not attend such meetings, as they were held behind closed doors and nobody was admitted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, based on your earlier answers you have just referred to military representatives, representatives of NATO would the same hold true when General Delic met with any HV or HVO Generals outside or other military leaders outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, I did not attend -- as a rule I did not attend such meetings and would not be present in the room where they were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I guess the final question in this series would be, sir, foreign political or civilian authorities, when General Delic was travelling outside of Bosnia and Herzegovina and met with foreign diplomats or political or civilian leaders were you ever personally present in the room when those meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No I was never present during discussions, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So based on these answers it would be fair to say, would it not, that throughout the time-period that you were serving as General Delic's body-guard, you were never present personally at any meeting that General Delic had with any military or civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never attended these discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to another subject, and that has to do, sir, with your duties or responsibilities. Can you tell a little bit about what your duties entailed during the time-period that you served as an escort or body-guard for General Delic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The duties included providing security for the commander while in a location or on the move, and therefore those were my duties to provide security for the commander while in a location or on the move.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you some peripheral questions on these duties because based on the answers that you gave to my learned colleague Madam Vidovic it seemed that you did a few other things as well, and I'd like to ask you if you could perhaps clarify some of these things for us. You seem to imply, sir, that when you were in Malaysia with General Delic, in the autumn of 1995, that you would have been the person who would have dialed the telephone for him because General Delic doesn't speak English. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it was a bit unclear from where I'm sitting anyway whether you would have done that telephone dialing because of the fact that General Delic doesn't speak English or was it because of reasons concerning protocol?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, it was for security reasons. It meant the opening -- it meant that there was an open line, that could be eavesdropped and that was to be avoided. So it depended on who was on the other end of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand your answer, to be quite frank. Let me try to see if I can understand what you're saying. My question, sir, was really whether you were doing the dialing of the telephone because of the fact that General Delic didn't speak English or was it because of issues involving protocol and now you have raised security concerns about open telephone lines. Can you perhaps tell us exactly why it was that you would have been involved in dialing a telephone number from Malaysia, if any phone calls were made?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: From the security aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, if you're concerns, sir, were security, what difference would it have made whether you were on the phone or General Delic was on the phone? I don't understand -- I don't understand what the difference would be. If you were concerned about open phone lines, what difference does it make who was on the phone?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was up to the security assessment, to see who the conversation would take place with whether it was going to be with the command whether it was going to be the office since it was an open line that is eavesdropped and important matters should not be discussed over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think we all understand that, sir. But my question really was and I would like to focus your attention on this period when you were in Malaysia with General Delic. Can you tell us how it was that you would make a security assessment concerning whether or not the phone lines were secure?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: That was part of my job. That was my -- one of my duties. Precisely that, to assess security. Based on my security assessment as to whether the line was safe or not, the contact was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you this: When you were on this mission or trip to Malaysia with General Delic who else was present, other than the two of you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: It was a large delegation, including representatives of the politics. We had journalists Senad Kamenica, Dr. Bosanko Horozic, who were also with us. And I can't remember all the names of those who were a part of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think the witness said there was a journalist whose name was Senad -- could you recall the name of the journalist?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Senad Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, other than yourself and General Delic, who else in the delegation was a member of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: General Delic's son, Admir Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Anyone else that you remember?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who else was part of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me ask you about this security assessment concerning the phone line. What steps, if any, did you take to make this security assessment concerning the phone line while you were in Malaysia?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the lines were open lines, we did not make contact with Sarajevo or any other centres in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Other than that, we didn't have portable phones or satellite phone that would enable to us establish safer connections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you stay in Malaysia when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We were accommodated in a hotel that I can't remember in Kuala Lumpur. I know we were in Kuala Lumpur.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's for the moment -- let's leave Malaysia behind us. When you were travelling with General Delic in Bosnia and Herzegovina, what type of security assessments did you make concerning communication systems? We'll start with communication systems in general.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which communication systems you have in mind. Is it telephone systems, radio relay systems? What exactly are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start with telephone systems. What steps did you take as General Delic's body-guard to make security assessments concerning telephone lines that General Delic might have used?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The telephone lines -- well, the telephone lines were pretty bad. All the information, all the information, the phone-tapping, this was something that we received all the information through the communication service. At that point in time we had a very bad communication system. The telephones and the radio relay devices were outdated and the aggressor of course had devices with which at any point in time they to listen in to the telephones and to the radio relay devices, and they were covering that at all times; and they were eavesdropping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, about any type of satellite phones or mobile phones that General Delic might have had during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: We never had satellite telephones or portable telephone devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ever during the course of the war. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, throughout the war we did not have such kind of devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about a few of your other duties in the time remaining for us today. You told us -- or in response to a question from my learned colleague from the Defence, you mentioned that you were carrying General Delic's brief case. Do you remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was that something that you normally would have had to do as part of his security detail, carry bags?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not to carry his bags. I carried his personal brief case, in which he carried his -- well, in which he kept his notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. In response to a question I believe from the Presiding Judge, you told us that, at least with respect to this trip to Malaysia, that General Delic did not have any maps in his personal brief case. Is that -- is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my answer. General Delic did not take any maps with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did your duties, sir, entail packing General Delic's personal brief case?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would prepare the things that the commander would take with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how would you know what things the commander wanted to take with him?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: The commander would tell me which things he needed, so I would get that ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what were your duties, if any, concerning handling of documents that were addressed to General Delic? Did you have any responsibility concerning documents addressed to General Delic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any contacts with the documents or any documentation that was sent to General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're then clear, sir, on no occasion, to the best of your recollection, did you ever hand General Delic any documents coming from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I personally did not hand to the commander any document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't know what documents General Delic may have been handed or not, because you weren't involved in personally handed documents to him.

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not take part in that. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you told us earlier today, Mr. Dedovic, or you've spent actually a good part of your testimony today talking about where you and General Delic travelled to during the course of the war. Did you keep, sir, any kind of diary indicating where you were at various points in time during the war?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never kept any kind of diary with dates and places that we visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How about any kind of official log-book? Did you maintain, as part of your duties or responsibilities, any kind of log-book or official document, official document that would have indicated where General Delic was travelling?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not have to maintain such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why not? There was no requirement?

utterances.speaker: ISMET DEDOVIC
utterances.text: That's true, there was no requirement. I did not have to keep any records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I think this would be a convenient spot perhaps to adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. We will adjourn for today, to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in the same court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of April, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.57 p.m.,
